meta.title: Add Controller or NVMe to VM | ProxMenux Documentation
meta.description: PCI passthrough of a storage controller (SATA / SAS HBA) or NVMe device to a Proxmox VM using ProxMenux. Handles IOMMU enablement, conflict detection and qm set --hostpci wiring.
meta.ogTitle: Add Controller or NVMe to VM | ProxMenux Documentation
meta.ogDescription: Pass a whole SATA / SAS HBA or NVMe device into a Proxmox VM. ProxMenux handles IOMMU, conflict detection and hostpci wiring.

header.title: Add Controller or NVMe to VM
header.description: Pass a whole SATA / SAS host bus adapter (HBA) or NVMe device into a Proxmox VM via PCI passthrough. ProxMenux checks and — with your consent — enables IOMMU, enumerates the passthrough-eligible devices, filters out conflicts and wires the assignment with qm set --hostpci.

intro.title: What this does (and does not) do
intro.body: This is device-level passthrough: the PCIe card leaves the host kernel's view and is bound to vfio-pci. The VM sees the controller itself — not the individual disks behind it — and loads its own driver for that exact model. Every disk attached to that controller follows it automatically, with native SMART data, full firmware features and no Proxmox layer in between.

howRuns.heading: How the script runs
howRuns.body: The flow has two phases with clear separation between "collecting information, checking IOMMU and listing candidates" and "actually attaching the PCI device". Until the final confirmation nothing is written to the VM config.

iommu.heading: IOMMU groups — why the whole card leaves at once
iommu.body: The isolation boundary for PCI passthrough is the IOMMU group, the smallest unit the CPU’s IOMMU can isolate. Devices in the same group cannot be isolated from each other. If a SATA controller shares its group with a USB controller, passing through SATA may also require releasing USB from the host, or may prevent passthrough. It does not automatically assign every device in the group to the VM.
iommu.outro: ProxMenux does not check IOMMU groups. Before you pass a card through, check its group with the manual commands below: if the group holds more than the controller you want, the other devices leave the host with it.

prereqs.heading: Prerequisites
items: CPU and motherboard support VT-d (Intel) or AMD-Vi, and it is enabled in firmware (BIOS/UEFI). ProxMenux can enable the kernel side for you, but it cannot flip the firmware switch.
The target VM is powered off before attaching PCI devices.
The target VM uses the q35 machine type. ProxMenux rejects other machine types.
The controller/NVMe is not the one holding the Proxmox root filesystem. The script hides anything in use by the host.
Guest OS has drivers for the controller model. Linux covers virtually every HBA out of the box; Windows needs the vendor driver installed before you boot with the controller attached.
prereqs.warnBody: A VM with PCI passthrough is tied to the node that physically holds the card. Live migration across nodes will fail. Plan backups / replication accordingly.

list.title: Pick the target VM
list.bodyRich: ProxMenux reads qm list and shows every VM with its status and machine type. Pick the one that will receive the controller. A running VM, or one whose machine type is not q35, is rejected.
list.caption: VM selection dialog

list.title: IOMMU check
list.bodyRich: If IOMMU is not active, ProxMenux offers to enable it. It edits /etc/kernel/cmdline (for systemd-boot) or /etc/default/grub (for GRUB), appends the parameters for your CPU and runs proxmox-boot-tool refresh or update-grub:
list.outro: The flow continues and the devices are assigned in the same run, but the host must reboot before the VM starts. At the end ProxMenux offers to reboot now; if you decline, do not start the VM until the host has rebooted.
list.caption: IOMMU Required — offer to enable and reboot

list.title: Device enumeration
list.body: ProxMenux lists every storage-class PCI device (SATA / SAS / RAID HBAs and NVMe). For each device it shows:
items: Assigned to VM when another VM already has the device in its config.
A ⚠ marker when a disk behind the controller is referenced in a stopped VM or CT config.
list.caption: Controller / NVMe device enumeration

list.title: Conflict detection
list.bodyRich: Controllers with a disk that holds the Proxmox system or is used by a running VM or CT are hidden for safety and listed in the dialog, and so are devices already in the target VM. SR-IOV virtual functions, and physical functions with active VFs, are excluded after selection. If another VM already has the device, a running owner blocks it; for a stopped owner you choose to keep it there with onboot disabled, move it to the target VM or skip it. Disks referenced in stopped VM or CT configs get a similar choice: disable onboot, remove the references or leave them as they are.
list.caption: Conflict detection — device blocked with reason

list.title: Attach and finalise
list.bodyRich: ProxMenux shows a summary with a compatibility notice (on some platforms the host slows down or freezes when the VM starts; old firmware and low-power CPUs are flagged). On confirm, for every selected device it runs qm set <VMID> --hostpciN <pci-addr>,pcie=1, choosing the next free hostpci slot. If IOMMU was enabled during this session, it offers to reboot the host.
list.caption: Assignment summary — hostpciN slots and PCI addresses attached

troubleshoot.heading: Troubleshooting
troubleshoot.noGroupsTitle: IOMMU enabled but no groups under /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/
troubleshoot.noGroupsBody: Reboot is required for the kernel cmdline to take effect. If the groups are still missing after reboot, VT-d / AMD-Vi is probably disabled in firmware — check the BIOS/UEFI setup.
troubleshoot.busyTitle: VM fails to start with "hostpciN: device busy"
troubleshoot.busyBody: Another process still holds the PCI device. Most common causes: a previous VM that crashed without releasing it, or the host kernel reclaimed it on the last boot. Run lspci -nnk -s <addr> to see which driver is bound; it should be vfio-pci. A full host reboot usually clears this.
troubleshoot.noDisksTitle: Guest sees the controller but not the disks
troubleshoot.noDisksBody: The controller model lacks an in-guest driver. Linux almost never hits this; Windows does — install the vendor driver (e.g. LSI / Broadcom for older SAS HBAs) while the card is detached, then reboot with the card attached.
troubleshoot.sharedTitle: The IOMMU group includes an unrelated device
troubleshoot.sharedBody: Options: (a) move the card to a different PCIe slot to change its group, (b) enable ACS override in the kernel to split groups (security trade-off — research before applying), or (c) pick a different card in a cleaner group.
